title: PROSPECT-S: A Model for Spike Optical Properties Considering Winter Wheat Growth Dynamics
abstract: As the primary reproductive organ of winter wheat, the spike plays a crucial role in grain production, with its optical spectrum reflecting a combination of biochemical properties and morphological structures. Structural modifications, particularly spike width expansion, in wheat spikes induced by developmental progression, make it necessary to develop a spectral model that can respond to structural changes due to winter wheat growth dynamics and is applicable to the entire life cycle of wheat spikes. In this study, we developed PROSPECT-S, a spectral model that accounts for the effects of the dynamic growth of spikes on the structural characteristics, including structural parameter ( N s ) and refractive index ( nr ). Together with key biochemical parameters, including chlorophyll content ( C ab ), equivalent water thickness ( C w ), and dry matter content ( C m ), the model jointly characterized the optical properties of winter wheat spikes across the spectral range of 400 to 2,500 nm. The model’s performance was evaluated using actual spike measurements. The results demonstrated a strong agreement between the simulated and observed spike spectra across all phenological stages (validation accuracy: R 2 = 0.92, root mean square error = 0.052, normalized root mean square error = 0.205). Furthermore, our results indicate that PROSPECT-S can be effectively combined with measured spike spectra to accurately estimate key functional traits from the flowering stage to the grain filling stage, such as C ab , C w , and C m . Overall, the PROSPECT-S model, which could respond to the dynamic growth of the spike, provides a robust physics-based approach for accurately simulating spike spectra and retrieving key spike functional traits from hyperspectral measurements.

title: This Is APEX: An Active–Passive Remote Sensing Fusion Algorithm for 3-Dimensional Aerosol Extinction Coefficient Mapping and Regional Planetary Boundary Layer Height Estimation
abstract: The aerosol extinction coefficient (AEX), particularly in 3 dimensions (3D-AEX), is crucial for understanding aerosol–boundary layer interactions and improving climate models. However, existing remote sensing techniques, such as spaceborne active remote sensing with limited spatial coverage and passive remote sensing lacking vertical profiling, present challenges in obtaining high-resolution 3D-AEX fields. To address these challenges, this study proposes an advanced active–passive fusion algorithm for 3D aerosol extinction coefficient mapping (APEX) that integrates vertical profiles from a spaceborne high-spectral-resolution lidar (Aerosol and Carbon Dioxide Detection Lidar/Atmospheric Environment Monitoring Satellite) with aerosol optical depth and multichannel spectral data from geostationary satellites (Advanced Himawari Imager/Himawari-8 and Advanced Baseline Imager/Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite-16), generating high-resolution 3D-AEX fields with 5-km horizontal and 48-m vertical resolutions. The algorithm employs an iterative optimization strategy with geometry-based distance threshold adjustment to improve stability over long distances and integrates spatial-distance and spectral-similarity weights to reduce the reliance on spatial proximity alone in selecting representative neighboring profiles. The algorithm demonstrates substantial improvements, with the dead zone reconstruction achieving an R 2 of 0.7718 within 50 km and 0.6155 within 200 km, outperforming fixed threshold methods by 11.08%. Space–ground validation yields an average root mean squared error of 0.0298 km −1 , comparable to ground-based measurement errors. Furthermore, the retrieved planetary boundary layer height from the 3D-AEX fields, with a resolution of 5 km, represents a 5-fold improvement over data from the fifth generation of ECMWF atmospheric reanalyses for climate (ERA5). This algorithm provides a high-resolution 3D framework for analyzing aerosol–boundary layer interactions, offering valuable data support for climate models and atmospheric studies.

title: Satellite Remote Sensing of Global Ecosystem Water Use Efficiency: Accuracies, Patterns, and Drivers
abstract: Ecosystem water use efficiency (eWUE), the ratio of gross primary production (GPP) to evapotranspiration (ET), characterizes the carbon–water trade-off in terrestrial ecosystems. However, the global spatiotemporal patterns of eWUE and their dominant drivers remain insufficiently understood. This study comprehensively validated 64 remote sensing (RS)-derived eWUEs against observations from 67 flux towers. We subsequently utilized the 9 highest-performing eWUEs and 3 widely used eWUEs (MODIS, FLUXCOM, and GLASS) to investigate the spatiotemporal patterns and dominant drivers of global eWUE from 2001 to 2015. Results indicated that most RS eWUEs underestimated ground observations, along with substantial accuracy divergence (root mean square error: 1.23 to 1.83 g C/kg H 2 O monthly; 0.75 to 1.56 g C/kg H 2 O annually). Notably, eWUEs derived from carbon–water coupled products (PMLv2 and BESSv2) outperformed those from independent GPP and ET products. The top 9 eWUEs exhibited broadly consistent global spatial patterns of multiyear means. In contrast, the 3 widely used eWUEs exhibited substantial divergence: GLASS and FLUXCOM yielded systematically lower values, while MODIS presented a distinct spatial distribution inconsistent with the top-performing eWUEs. From 2001 to 2015, statistically significant increasing trends were observed in 5 of the top 9 eWUEs, whereas only one exhibited a significant decline. Moreover, leaf area index was identified as the dominant driver of eWUE variations for 8 of the top 9 eWUEs. This study provides an essential reference for selecting RS products to derive eWUE and advances our understanding of the spatiotemporal patterns and dominant drivers of global eWUE.

title: DEDM-Net: Diffusion-Enhanced Dense Mamba Network for Infrared Small Target Detection
abstract: Infrared small target detection plays a pivotal role in remote sensing situational awareness, forest fire prevention, and surveillance and early warning systems. Current mainstream deep learning methods, however, primarily focus on target-specific features while underutilizing the nontarget background regions. Furthermore, extremely small-scale targets are often undetectable due to the difficulty of extracting their feature information. To address these challenges, we propose a Diffusion-Enhanced Dense Mamba Network for small target detection. The network comprises 2 main stages: a feature enhancement stage based on the dual-path diffusion model and a target detection stage based on the dense link state space model. In the feature enhancement stage, the diffusion model, combined with low-frequency image features and a blind processing module, performs dual-path modeling of target-free backgrounds and candidate target masks, effectively enhancing target features while mitigating background clutter. In the target detection stage, the state space model captures long-range correlations across both global and local features. Utilizing a dense link nested structure along with a cross-stage prediction fusion module, features of different scales, semantics, and stages are thoroughly integrated and enhanced, enabling effective detection of weak and small infrared targets. Experimental results on 3 publicly available high-quality datasets demonstrate that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in detection probability, intersection over union, and other evaluation metrics compared with other advanced methods.

title: Active Remote Sensing Reflectance Measurement Using White-Light Lidar: Monte Carlo Simulations
abstract: Remote-sensing reflectance ( R rs ) is a fundamental parameter in ocean-color remote sensing. A new active and direct approach for measuring R rs using white-light lidar spanning 400 to 720 nm is proposed, and its feasibility is investigated through radiative-transfer simulations under the assumption of optically homogeneous water bodies. The results demonstrate that the fraction of multiple scattering in the lidar signal is the dominant factor controlling the measurement accuracy of R rs . Under calm sea-surface conditions and Chl between 0.01 and 5.00 mg/m 3 , simulations show that the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of R rs measurements stays below 10% when the receiving footprint is large enough. This requirement is readily met for an airborne platform at a detection altitude (H) of 3,000 m with a receiver field of view (FOV) greater than 20 mrad, and even for a spaceborne platform at H = 500 km with FOV = 0.5 mrad. By contrast, low-altitude platforms suffer from markedly increased errors due to insufficient collection of multiple-scattered photons. Further analysis indicates that water inherent optical properties (IOPs) influence measurement performance by modulating photon step size and the number of scattering events, resulting in necessitating larger receiving footprints in clearer waters and in blue-green bands. Among the representative scattering phase functions (SPFs) examined, SPF effects are relatively minor. A preprocessing strategy that truncates near-surface signals is further proposed to suppress sea-surface-reflection interference. These findings provide guidance for optimizing white-light lidar systems for active R rs measurement and for supporting ocean-color satellite calibration.

title: Fine-Scale Mapping of Global Wetland Cities under the Ramsar System: An Object-Knowledge-Based 3-Stage Hierarchical Optimization Cascade Method
abstract: Ramsar Wetland Cities (RWCs) is a global paradigm for harmonizing urban development with wetland conservation, hosting wetland ecosystems of important representative value. However, the failure of existing wetland products to comprehensively encompass the Ramsar classification system hinders rigorous accreditation and renewal evaluation. To fill this gap, this study developed the Object-Knowledge-based Hierarchical Optimization Cascade method, utilizing Sentinel-1/2 time series imagery aligned with the 5 accreditation and renewal key nodes of RWCs (2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, and 2024). The Object-Knowledge-based Hierarchical Optimization Cascade method employs a hierarchical extraction strategy: First, an optimized Random Forest model separates wetlands from nonwetlands based on spectral separability; subsequently, fine wetland types are delineated by integrating geometric features and seasonal inundation variations. For complex wetland classes during the subdivision process, cascaded spectral clustering and XGBoost algorithm are applied to enable nonlinear decision making for enhanced precision. Furthermore, a geometric similarity inheritance was introduced to ensure reliable temporal migration for complex wetland types. Consequently, we produced the first Global Wetland City Fine Classification System 10-m product, distinguishing 18 Ramsar wetland classes and 6 nonwetland classes. Results indicate that Global Wetland City Fine Classification System 10-m product achieves an overall classification accuracy of 94.98%. The dataset reveals a net increase of approximately 145,781.41 ha in wetland area across 43 RWCs globally from 2016 to 2024, with a total area reaching 3,063,592.66 ha by 2024, corroborating the positive protective efficacy of RWC accreditation. This dataset is publicly available, serving as a robust resource for RWC monitoring, ecological evaluating, international strategic indicator assessment, and sustainable management.

title: Antagonistic Roles of Climate Change and Human Activities in Reshaping Yangtze River Turbidity Revealed by a Virtual Satellite Constellation
abstract: The Yangtze River, one of the world’s largest river systems, plays a vital role in regional ecological security. However, monitoring its turbidity dynamics remains difficult. Most satellite-based algorithms are designed for lakes or estuaries and often fail in narrow, optically complex rivers. Moreover, the temporal resolution constraints of individual satellites are insufficient to resolve the rapid short-term variability in rivers (e.g., 8 days for Landsat-8/9). To address these challenges, we developed a virtual satellite constellation by integrating Landsat-8/9 and Sentinel-2 imagery (2013 to 2023), reconstructing a high-resolution turbidity dataset for the Yangtze River. We built sensor-specific support vector regression models ( R 2 = 0.74 and 0.66 and root mean square error [RMSE] = 16.62 and 17.74 Nephelometric Turbidity Units (NTU) for Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8/9, respectively), which outperformed other algorithms. An empirical cross-sensor harmonization method further reduced inter-mission biases (RMSE = 15.45 ± 13.43 NTU; symmetric mean absolute percentage error = 12.53% ± 15.98%). This constellation improved temporal resolution from 5 to 16 days to 2.5 days on average. The reconstructed dataset revealed a mean turbidity of 67.75 ± 58.35 NTU, with significant seasonal (wet > dry) and spatial patterns (reaches on the Qinghai–Xizang Plateau > mid-lower reaches > cascade reservoirs). Over the past decade, trends diverged sharply: turbidity increased in reaches on the Qinghai–Xizang Plateau (8.12 ± 5.51 NTU year −1 ) due to climate-induced warming and enhanced runoff accelerating erosion, but declined in cascade reservoirs (−3.40 ± 3.17 NTU year −1 ) and mid-lower reaches (−2.06 ± 1.04 NTU year −1 ) because of sediment trapping and ecological restoration. This study establishes a framework for high-frequency river water quality monitoring and highlights the antagonistic effects of climate change and human activity on sediment dynamics.

title: Toward High-Accuracy Coastal Sea Surface Salinity Retrieval: A Dual-Pathway Framework from Interferometric Radiometry to Physical Forward Modeling
abstract: Currently, spaceborne L-band radiometers struggle to deliver accurate, high-resolution coastal salinity products. We outline a dual-pathway framework that incorporates measurement cleaning and forward-model deepening for next-generation coastal sea surface salinity (SSS) retrieval. Furthermore, a set of priorities guides the design and development of coastal SSS retrieval systems for the next decade.

title: Improving Soybean Yield Estimation by Incorporating Angular Anisotropy in Physics-Guided Deep Learning
abstract: Accurate soybean yield estimation requires the effective fusion of solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF), which is a key indicator of photosynthetic function, and structural information from reflectance-based vegetation indices. However, both SIF and vegetation indices are subject to Sun–sensor geometry, and robust multisource integration that exploits canopy directional signatures remains challenging. To address this issue, we propose M-Net, a physics-guided deep learning framework that explicitly incorporates canopy angular anisotropy for yield prediction. Instead of treating angular effects as noise to be normalized, M-Net incorporates bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF)-derived angular features into an attention-based architecture to encode 3-dimensional canopy angular anisotropy as predictive information. Sensitivity analysis demonstrated that the accuracy of yield estimation decreased as Sun–sensor geometries deviated from the nadir, a trend particularly pronounced for physiological SIF signals susceptible to angular distortion. In comparative experiments, standard recurrent baselines (e.g., gated recurrent unit and long short-term memory) gained little from physics-reconstructed angular anisotropy features. In contrast, M-Net effectively used these anisotropic signatures and converted canopy directional anisotropy into predictive information. Validated across 613 US soybean-growing counties (2019 to 2023), M-Net achieved a high accuracy ( R 2 = 0.69). Notably, yield estimation using coarse-resolution Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer data with BRDF-derived multiangular canopy anisotropy features ( R 2 = 0.64) outperformed that of high-resolution Sentinel-2 data with fixed viewing angles ( R 2 = 0.56), suggesting that effectively using angular information may be more important than spatial resolution alone. The results demonstrate that physics-guided deep learning transforms angular anisotropy from uncertainty into a valuable predictive signal, providing a practical approach for multisource crop monitoring.

title: Top 10 Frontier Scientific Challenges in the Field of Remote Sensing Science and Technology
A Prototype Precipitation Retrieval Algorithm for Passive Microwave Observations from the FY-3G Satellite
abstract: Precipitation products retrieved from satellite-based passive microwave observations are essential for understanding global water and energy cycles. This study develops a prototype retrieval algorithm for passive microwave observations from FY-3G satellite, based on a Bayesian framework with a unique a priori database constructed using a 1-dimensional variational method. The algorithm is further applied to generate an operational multiple-hydrometeor profile (MHP) product. The performance of the MHP product is evaluated against 2 representative products derived via the Goddard profiling algorithm (GPROF) and the combined radar-radiometer algorithm (CMB). Case studies show good agreement in the spatial distribution patterns of surface precipitation rate, rainwater path, and ice water path across the 3 products, while MHP’s cloud liquid water path pattern more closely resembles precipitation intensity than those from GPROF and CMB. Statistical analysis indicates that the MHP surface precipitation rate values align well with GPROF and CMB, with relative biases generally within ±14% over both ocean and land. MHP underestimates oceanic rainwater path by 27% and 19% relative to GPROF and CMB, respectively, while land estimates lie in between. For ice water path, MHP consistently yields smaller values than GPROF but larger than CMB, primarily due to differences in ice microphysical assumptions. Notably, MHP exhibits a markedly stronger cloud liquid water path-precipitation intensity correlation than the other 2 products. These results highlight the high accuracy of the MHP product and suggest potential applicability of the proposed algorithm on other microwave imagers of FY-3 series, particularly for future missions.

title: Integrating Hyperspectral Data and Google Satellite Embedding Features for Aquatic Fish Biodiversity Prediction
abstract: Timely and reliable prediction of fish biodiversity across extensive river systems is pivotal for biodiversity monitoring and sustaining ecosystem stability. However, large-scale field surveys remain difficult, and broadband multispectral imagery captures habitat attributes only coarsely, limiting predictive precision. To address these challenges, Sentinel-2 multispectral observations, Gaofen-5A hyperspectral imagery, and the Google Satellite Embedding dataset were integrated with environmental DNA metabarcoding, and 7 machine learning algorithms were implemented to predict fish taxonomic diversity. A total of 149 environmental DNA samples were compiled from field campaigns and literature sources across 15 river basins in China. Habitat-informative vegetation indices were derived from pixel-level spectra, and 4 feature categories were examined, namely, multispectral variables, hyperspectral indices, deep embeddings, and fusion features combining hyperspectral information with satellite embeddings. Hyperspectral indices markedly improved prediction accuracy relative to that of Sentinel-2 multispectral predictors, achieving an R 2 of 0.80 ± 0.03 compared with 0.65 ± 0.07 for the multispectral baseline. Model performance remained stable across spectral resolutions using Gaofen-5A data. Notably, deep embedding features enabled multiple models to achieve an R 2 above 0.90, reflecting their strong capacity to integrate multisource information and characterize fish habitat conditions. Fusion of hyperspectral and embedding features produced the most accurate estimates of fish taxonomic richness with R 2 up to 0.94 ± 0.01. Overall, these outcomes demonstrate the feasibility and robustness of combining hyperspectral data with deep learned representations to predict riverine fish taxonomic richness, providing a multisource remote sensing pathway for biodiversity assessments across large spatial extents.

title: Impacts of Compound Drought–Fire Events on Vegetation Sensitivity to Precipitation: Evidence from Global Satellite Observations during 2005 to 2021
abstract: Vegetation sensitivity to precipitation (Sppt), which describes how vegetation photosynthesis responds to precipitation variability, is a key indicator of how terrestrial carbon–water cycles respond to precipitation variability. However, under the intensifying impacts of compound disturbances such as droughts and fires, its response remains not well understood. Here, we used satellite-derived vegetation proxies, including solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence, the normalized difference vegetation index, and the enhanced vegetation index, to assess the responses of Sppt under compound drought-fire disturbances. In terms of interannual variability, global Sppt declined from 2001 to 2022. However, following compound drought–fire events (2005 to 2021), growing-season Sppt increased across most regions within 1 and 3 years after the disturbances, showing a significantly stronger rise than under single drought events. The burned area of compound hydrological drought–fire events was larger, and their enhancement of Sppt was stronger than that of compound meteorological drought–fire events. Using an interpretable random forest model, we further identified that this increased Sppt was likely associated with atmospheric aridity and soil nutrient conditions, particularly nitrogen and phosphorus content. Nevertheless, after both compound hydrological drought–fire and compound meteorological drought–fire disturbances, the elevated Sppt was accompanied by a reduction in water use efficiency, suggesting a potential decoupling of ecosystem carbon–water coupling processes. Our results highlight that compound disturbances may increase the dependence of ecosystem photosynthetic carbon uptake on precipitation and raise the risk of carbon–water decoupling, potentially reducing vegetation resilience under future drought–fire regimes.

title: Anthropogenic Disturbance Dampens Climate-Driven Greening in the Arctic
abstract: Arctic vegetation is a critical component of the Earth system, regulating high-latitude carbon balance, surface energy exchange, and ecosystem resilience. Despite the widespread greening observed under recent warming, Arctic vegetation responses to the combined pressures of accelerating climate change and expanding human activity remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to anticipate future ecosystem trajectories and climate feedbacks. Here, by integrating 2 decades of 30-m Landsat observations with a novel attribution framework, we disentangled the respective contributions of climatic forcing and anthropogenic disturbance to vegetation dynamics within human footprint areas (HFAs) across the circumarctic. Based on 2,221 distinct HFA clusters, we found that while climatic warming has broadly enhanced vegetation greenness, anthropogenic disturbance has imposed strong, spatially concentrated browning, explaining 16.1% of the observed total greenness variability within HFAs. These disturbance effects are most pronounced in industrial and mining regions and intensify toward lower latitudes. Our findings reveal that human activity is emerging as an important modifier of Arctic vegetation dynamics, highlighting the need for disturbance-aware monitoring and adaptive management to sustain ecological integrity across the vulnerable Arctic.

title: A Remote Sensing-Based Solution for National Scale Tree Counting
abstract: Accurate tree counts are crucial for global restoration efforts, given the need for progress tracking and effective evaluation of tree planting and survival. However, conventional methods often fail to accurately capture tree counts at large scales, particularly in landscapes outside forests. We developed a deep learning approach for estimating tree counts from satellite imagery, nationally, across Rwanda and Tanzania in East Africa in 2019. We used a 20-band composite image composed of bands from PlanetScope, Sentinel-1, and Sentinel-2 as input, and estimated a total count of about 5.2 billion trees across the 2 countries. Only about 48.8% of the estimated tree counts fall within the WorldCover “tree cover” class, with the remainder being distributed across nonforest landscapes. Our work provides information on tree counts at the national scale in Rwanda and Tanzania using low-cost and freely available satellite images, which can guide the planning and optimization of resource allocation for tree restoration efforts at national scales.

title: Forest Height Regulates the Relationship between Sun-Induced Chlorophyll Fluorescence and Gross Primary Productivity at the Global Scale
abstract: Satellite sun-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) has emerged as a powerful proxy with great potential for tracking global vegetation photosynthesis. Yet, structural heterogeneity within vegetation canopies complicates the translation of SIF into gross primary productivity (GPP). In this study, we integrate global multi-source datasets with a SIF angular normalization theory incorporating a 2-leaf modeling strategy to investigate how forest height regulates the SIF-GPP linkage at the global scale. We show that increasing forest height systematically decreases the escape probability of SIF photons, thereby weakening the observed SIF signals. Simultaneously, taller canopies shift the balance between sunlit and shaded leaf contributions, affecting both SIF emission and GPP partitioning. These findings highlight the dual role of forest height in modulating both the radiative transfer of SIF and the physiological partitioning of GPP. Our results emphasize the necessity of integrating forest height into satellite-based photosynthesis models and provide a theoretical and observational basis for refining GPP estimates from spaceborne SIF measurements.

title: Regional Atmospheric Profile Retrieval Driven by Multistation Collaboration based on Geoscience-Informed Deep Learning
abstract: Accurate retrieval of atmospheric temperature and humidity profiles is essential for improving numerical weather prediction and climate simulations. However, the uneven distribution of ground-based radiometer stations creates data gaps, limiting the accuracy and spatial adaptability of existing inversion models. To address this challenge, we propose CTDformer (Convolutional Neural Network [CNN]–Transformer–DualBranchMLP), a multimodel learning framework that combines convolution-based feature extraction, attention-based sequence learning, and a dual-branch multilayer perception to retrieve vertical profiles over the Xi’an region. CTDformer incorporates spatial features such as station encoding, geographic coordinates, and interstation distances to enhance representational capacity and generalization. Experiments at 4 stations demonstrate that CTDformer outperforms individual models, reducing temperature and humidity profile errors by 7.64% and 5.31%, respectively. Incorporating spatial information into networked training further decreases errors by more than 7%. On 2021 May 15, the results indicate that CTDformer is more sensitive in capturing the buildup of convective energy, yielding substantially higher convective available potential energy than both the fifth-generation European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts atmospheric reanalysis and the single-station scheme prior to precipitation. It better aligns with the observed convective development and highlights its potential for severe convection monitoring and forecasting. This study addresses the challenges of sparse ground-based radiometric observations and limited model spatial generalization. By leveraging multistation collaboration, it achieves high-precision atmospheric profile retrieval of region, thereby enhancing diagnostic and early-warning capabilities for extreme weather, smog, and precipitation events. It can also offer reliable data support for applications in intelligent meteorology, short-term forecasting, and climate monitoring.

title: UAV-Based SfM Photogrammetry for Bathymetric Terrain Extraction in Antarctic Shallow Bays Near China’s Qinling Station
abstract: High-resolution nearshore bathymetric terrain is the baseline data for understanding the ice–ocean interaction in the Antarctic and is crucial for the safe operation and maintenance of Antarctic research stations. Particularly, for shallow-water topography, traditional surveying methods are inefficient and costly, while satellite remote sensing techniques are limited by spatial resolution. Uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-based structure-from-motion (SfM) photogrammetry, as a high-efficiency and low-cost technique, provides new opportunities for coastal geomorphic research. However, refraction effect, floating ices, and large gravels pose challenges to bathymetric terrain extraction from UAV-based SfM photogrammetry in Antarctic gravel-bed bays. This study takes Seal Bay near the Qinling Station of China as an example and presents the workflow and applicability assessment for extracting bathymetric terrain of gravel-bed bays using UAV-SfM photogrammetry. This workflow utilizes UAV-captured overlapping images to reconstruct the initial dense point cloud, and accurate bathymetric digital terrain models are obtained by combining refraction correction and ground filtering methods. Validation against in situ uncrewed surface vehicle measurements shows that the R 2 (coefficient of determination) of small-angle refraction correction method is 0.83, with an RMSE (root mean square error) of 0.43 m, under nadir viewing angle conditions. Meanwhile, the classification accuracy of underwater terrain extraction with cloth simulation filtering for removing floating ices and gravels exceeds 97%. This study provides a cost-effective strategy for bathymetric terrain extraction that can easily be applied in other shallow gravel-bed bays along the Antarctic coastlines.

title: Self-Supervised Spatiotemporal Reconstruction of Ocean Color Chlorophyll-a from Satellite Observations
abstract: Satellite ocean color chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) records are heavily gapped due to clouds and orbital sampling, which can bias trend and phenology analyses and hinder studies of mesoscale dynamics. We present generalized data complementation model-empirical orthogonal function (GDCM-EOF), a self-supervised spatiotemporal gap-filling framework that learns to reconstruct missing Chl-a directly from partially observed satellite records, avoiding reliance on external reanalysis labels that are often unavailable or scale-mismatched for ocean color. The model combines (a) geolocation encoding to represent large-scale spatial gradients, (b) an EOF (empirical orthogonal function)-based low-rank modality enhancement that injects dominant-mode priors for background consistency, and (c) a stage-wise knowledge-transfer strategy with multiscale attention to improve robustness under extreme missingness. We train and evaluate on European Space Agency Ocean Colour Climate Change Initiative v6.0 daily Chl-a (1998 to 2017), using 1998 to 2014 for self-supervised training/validation and 2015 to 2017 as an independent test period. Experiments are conducted at 2 scales: a global 1° × 1° product over 60°S–60°N and a regional Caribbean Sea product at 0.04° × 0.04°. Using a withheld-observation protocol (15% withheld; 85% as input), GDCM-EOF consistently outperforms the classical data-interpolating empirical orthogonal function baseline: In the Caribbean test, root mean square error decreases from 0.107 to 0.019 and R 2 increases from 0.803 to 0.998; globally, root mean square error decreases from 0.110 to 0.066 and R 2 increases from 0.904 to 0.979. The reconstructions preserve large-scale background fields while recovering mesoscale structures such as tropical instability waves and estuarine–current interactions. Comparisons with the Copernicus-GlobColour gap-free product further support the physical plausibility of reconstructed patterns and enable improved analyses of spatial variability and long-term Chl-a trends.

title: Contrastive Learning with Spatial–Spectral Masking and Mixing for Hyperspectral Image Classification
abstract: Hyperspectral imagery, with its rich spatial and spectral information, has become a key tool for analyzing the semantic types of ground objects. The data-hungry nature of deep models, coupled with the high cost of label acquisition, presents a substantial challenge for the intelligent analysis of hyperspectral images. Existing methods mainly rely on a proxy task, such as contrastive learning, to pre-train deep models on unlabeled datasets, leveraging knowledge from unlabeled data to overcome the challenge. These methods focus on aligning samples with spatial transformations to learn spatially invariant features in the pre-training phase. While effective, they struggle to overcome inherent spectral variations, limiting classification accuracy. So, we propose a spatial–spectral masking contrastive learning strategy that forces the model to align semantically consistent samples with partial missing spatial and spectral information in the feature space, thus learning features invariant to spatial and spectral variations. Specifically, we design a spatial–spectral masking strategy, which maximizes the removal of redundant pixels and bands while ensuring semantic invariance, generating masked samples for contrastive learning. Additionally, we introduce a data augmentation technique, namely, proportional cross-sample mixing, which exploits potential relationships between different samples to enrich the training data. Considering the interference from background clutter, we develop a spatial–spectral decoupling framework that decouples the extraction of spectral and spatial features to ensure their sufficient and collaborative expression. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, with only 5 labels per class, our method achieves marked classification improvements on the Pavia University, Pavia Center, Yan Cheng, and Salinas datasets.

title: A Novel Approach to Retrieve River Water Levels by Decomposing Altimetry Waveforms
abstract: Although Sentinel-3 synthetic-aperture radar altimetry has improved along-track resolution, accurate water level retrieval over heterogeneous river systems remains constrained by the instrument’s pulse-limited across-track footprint. In complex hydrogeomorphological settings, lateral water bodies can generate strong competing returns despite antenna attenuation, potentially causing standard retrackers to erroneously lock onto these off-nadir interference signals. Addressing this, we propose a physics-based component-wise simulation framework to explicitly consider the ground heterogeneity within the footprint. Unlike traditional top-down empirical methods relying on waveform statistics, our bottom-up strategy integrates topography with water masks to reconstruct the observation geometry. We explicitly simulate backscatter contributions from spatially distinct water bodies, decomposing the received waveform into constituent river and interference components based on range and radiometric properties. Validation over the 55 virtual stations demonstrates that this source attribution method reduces the unbiased root-mean-square error from 0.79 m for the Offset Center of Gravity retracker to 0.47 m, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art retracking algorithms such as the Synthetic Aperture Radar Altimeter MOde Studies and Applications and modified Multiple Waveform Persistent Peak retrackers. Consequently, it effectively reconstructs continuous water level time series at highly complex reaches where observations are routinely discarded by operational databases (e.g., Database for Hydrological Time Series over Inland Waters and Hydroweb). We quantitatively demonstrate that off-nadir signal dominance is driven by the radiometric counterbalance between antenna gain attenuation and the high specular reflectivity of lateral water bodies. This framework establishes a rigorous physical approach for resolving composite synthetic-aperture radar echoes, extending the observational capabilities of current and future missions (e.g., Sentinel-3 and Sentinel-6) in spatially disjointed environments.

title: Flood capture: A new method relying on ground-based remote sensing and surveying
A Major Advancement in Nighttime Light Remote Sensing: Applications and Prospects of SDGSAT-1 Data
abstract: Rapid global urbanization poses unprecedented challenges to global sustainability. Since the 1990s, nighttime light (NTL) remote sensing has emerged as a key tool for monitoring urbanization and human activities. However, early-stage NTL datasets, such as those from the Defense Meteorological Satellite Program’s Operational Linescan System and the Suomi National Polar-Orbiting Partnership’s Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite, suffer from coarse spatial resolution and limited spectral information, hindering detailed urban analysis. Launched in 2021, the Sustainable Development Science Satellite 1 (SDGSAT-1), the world’s first science satellite dedicated to the United Nations 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), has greatly advanced NTL remote sensing by providing data at 10-m (panchromatic) and 40-m (RGB) spatial resolutions. In this review, we synthesize the applications of SDGSAT-1 NTL data in urban structure delineation, lighting classification, socioeconomic characterization, public perception analysis, and emergency assessment. We also discuss challenges (e.g., data noise and limited temporal coverage) and demands for novel street-level analysis methods alongside future directions. Beyond proposing application strategies such as integrating multimodal big data, establishing ground–aerial–orbital collaborative observation frameworks, decomposing NTL components, and developing multilayered NTL models, we outline several research directions that facilitate the transition from macroscale phenomenological descriptions to microscale mechanistic interpretations. Key areas include economic structure analysis, exploration of human–nature interactions, precision monitoring of the SDGs, and advancement of research on public health and social equity. This review offers a comprehensive overview of SDGSAT-1 NTL data applications and their potential in monitoring urban development and addressing the challenges of sustainable development.

title: Deep Learning-Based Precipitation Classification Using Global Precipitation Measurement Dual-Frequency Precipitation Radar
abstract: The Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) Dual-Frequency Precipitation Radar (DPR) is a cornerstone of meteorological and climate research. Current GPM data products classify precipitation types using threshold-based methods applied to dual-frequency measurements from vertical profiles of reflectivity (VPRs) and auxiliary parameters. While effective for operational classification, these methods rely on predefined decision rules that can be sensitive to calibration and environmental variability and may not capture the complex, nonlinear relationships present in precipitation structure, prompting interest in leveraging machine learning for improved classification. This study introduces a deep neural network (DNN) that utilizes statistically derived features as well as convolutional features extracted from VPRs as inputs. Using a novel labeling strategy based on data from the Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor network, the proposed model captures both the statistical and gradient patterns of precipitation for stratiform precipitation, snow, convective precipitation, and hail. For these 4 types, the DNN improves precision from 0.70 to 0.87 and recall from 0.67 to 0.88 relative to the GPM/DPR Version 07 product. These results demonstrate the DNN approach’s potential to provide an accurate solution aligned with the GPM mission to advance meteorological and climate research.

title: Deep Learning for Road Extraction with CHN10-CUG: A Large-Scale Benchmark and a Comprehensive Review
abstract: Understanding and modeling large-scale road networks under diverse geographic and environmental conditions remains a fundamental challenge for remote-sensing-based Earth observation. Existing reviews of deep-learning-based road extraction have largely focused on method-by-method summaries, with limited support from unified evaluation frameworks and sufficiently diverse real-world datasets for systematic methodological comparison and practical application. Moreover, existing public datasets are limited in diversity and fail to capture the complexity of heterogeneous landscapes, constraining the reliability and scalability of large-scale road mapping. Unlike prior works, this study makes 3 main contributions. First, we present CHN10-CUG, a new high-resolution dataset covering 10 representative Chinese cities, with detailed annotations of road surfaces, centerlines, and topological structures. Compared to existing datasets, CHN10-CUG offers richer spectral, textural, geometric, and topological diversity, supporting multitask road extraction across large and diverse regions. Second, we establish the first unified benchmark, rigorously reproducing and evaluating 15 widely used semantic segmentation models and 30 representative road-specific methods on CHN10-CUG, enabling reproducible performance comparison. Third, we conduct a comprehensive review of deep-learning-based road extraction, highlighting key advances, limitations, opportunities, and potential future directions for geoscience applications. Cross-regional transfer and long-term mapping experiments demonstrate that CHN10-CUG provides a challenging test bed for evaluating model robustness and generalization under fragmented and geographically heterogeneous conditions. These results highlight its potential to support scalable road mapping, multitask learning, and long-term infrastructure monitoring. By integrating dataset, benchmark, and review, this study provides a reproducible resource for remote sensing and Earth observation, with all datasets and codes openly released at https://github.com/CUG-URS/CHN10-CUG-Road-Benchmark-and-A-Comprehensive-Review .

title: Wetland Inundation Mapping through Geostatistical Data Fusion of Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and PlanetScope Machine Learning Classifications
abstract: Continuous, high-resolution inundation data are needed to understand how small-scale, short-term wetland flooding influences global methane emissions and carbon cycling. Small (<1,000 m 2 ), variably inundated wetlands are important methane sources, yet coarse satellite products often miss their dynamics. Integrating optical and radar imagery with resolutions <30 m offers a solution over single-sensor approaches, but 2 needs remain: (a) understanding the relative strengths and limitations of different sensors for detecting inundation in vegetated wetlands and (b) developing methods that leverage these sensor characteristics to transform sparse, irregular classification maps with different resolutions into complete, consistent coverage. To address this, we first evaluated sensors by classifying inundation from 2017 to 2022 across a wetland area in eastern North Carolina using Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and PlanetScope imagery. We used tree-based machine learning models to classify pixels as Dry Land, Inundated Vegetation, or Open Water and compared maps of inundation frequency produced by each model. Sentinel-2 random forest achieved the highest accuracy (93.9%) followed by the PlanetScope (88.4%) and Sentinel-1 (84.6%) models. Next, we introduced a fusion framework based on fixed-rank kriging, a spatiotemporal statistical model, to fuse binary classification maps into daily inundation probabilities at a 6-m resolution. The fused approach balanced individual sensor variability and detected short-term inundation fluctuations missed by the Landsat Dynamic Surface Water Extent, a widely used satellite-derived data product. By characterizing sensor performance and translating that information into a multisensor fusion approach, this work enables high-resolution, continuous monitoring of inundation dynamics vital to predicting wetland methane emissions.

title: Tracking the Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Center-Pivot Irrigation Systems in China (2000 to 2024) Using an Improved Deep Learning Framework
abstract: Center-pivot irrigation systems (CPISs) represent a water-efficient irrigation technology, yet their rapid expansion can exacerbate the trade-off between food production and groundwater sustainability in water-scarce regions. In China, the absence of continuous, long-term observations of CPISs has limited our ability to quantify this food–water trade-off. To address the challenges of CPIS extraction in heterogeneous agricultural landscapes, we propose an EfficientNet–UNet framework equipped with a focal Tversky loss and a PointRend (Point-based Rendering) refinement module (ETP-UNet). Experimental results demonstrate that ETP-UNet achieved an intersection over union (IoU) of 81.0%, an F1-score of 89.5%, and a boundary IoU of 66.0%. Using ETP-UNet, we generated a long-term China CPIS (CCPIS) dataset at 3-year intervals from 2000 to 2024, achieving overall accuracies above 0.88 and macro-F1-scores exceeding 0.87. A sample-based area estimator indicates that the CPIS area expanded from 23 ± 18 km 2 in 2000 to 2,202 ± 64 km 2 in 2024, representing an approximately 96-fold increase. This expansion was concentrated in semiarid regions and was most rapid during 2009 to 2015, coinciding with strengthened policy incentives for irrigation development. New CPISs were established predominantly on bare land (53%) and grassland (32%), with a smaller proportion from existing cropland (15%). CCPIS provides a critical foundation for jointly assessing CPIS-driven production gains and groundwater-depletion risks, supporting strategies that strengthen both food security and freshwater sustainability in arid and semiarid China.

title: National Mapping of Monoculture and Intercropped Maize via Phenology-Assisted Sampling: Application in Kenya
abstract: Monoculture and intercropped maize commonly coexist in smallholder-dominated regions like Kenya, forming the backbone of local food security. Alongside the prevalent focus on monoculture, intercropping can enhance agricultural sustainability and resilience but remains largely absent from remote sensing products and national statistics. This data gap, caused by spectral confusion, phenological variability, and field sample scarcity, limits effective agricultural policy formulation. To address this challenge, we developed the Phenology-assisted Sample generation for Monoculture and Intercropped Maize machine learning mapping (PSMIM) framework. PSMIM converts phenological knowledge into high-purity training samples through a 2-step hierarchical strategy: the variation of vegetation–pigment index first separates maize-dominated fields from nonmaize crops, and the water-to-greenness ratio then distinguishes monoculture from intercropped maize within relative phenological windows. These generated samples are integrated with random forest classification to combine the interpretability of phenology-based rules with the spectral–temporal learning capacity of machine learning. Ablation analysis confirmed that PSMIM achieved higher accuracy than rule-based thresholds and random forest trained only with limited field samples, demonstrating the contribution of phenology-assisted sample generation under label scarcity. Threshold zoning and sensitivity analyses further evaluated the adaptability and practical applicability of the sampling strategy across heterogeneous smallholder landscapes. Using PSMIM, we generated the first 10-m national maps of monoculture and intercropped maize for Kenya’s two 2023 to 2024 rainy seasons, achieving overall accuracies of 88.74% and 85.79%. The results provide a national-scale baseline for monitoring maize cropping patterns in Kenya and indicate the potential of PSMIM for food-security assessment in data-scarce smallholder regions.
